Stronger models benefit more from tool access, but reliable use of chemical software remains a challenge that Crucible Bench can track as models improve.

candidates.title: Detector Operating Behavior Inference via Data-Space Sampling
candidates.abstract: A detector scores candidate detections, but the recall and false alarms at a given confidence threshold depend on the input distribution. We introduce Detector Operating Behavior Inference (DOBI), a second-level inference task: estimating a fixed detector's threshold-dependent, distribution-level operating response from the internal evidence of a single unlabeled image. DOBI treats the detector's threshold response, i.e. recall, false positives, and precision across thresholds, as a latent behavioral state under the current data condition. Controlled data-space sampling probes this state space offline, and a lightweight monitor learns the inverse map from one image to this state, whose single functional output supports multiple operating policies. In a controlled proof of concept with a fixed YOLOv10-Nano person detector and COCO-derived degradations, predicted PR behavior reduces mean absolute deviation from 0.128 for an image-independent mean-behavior prior to 0.054, and predicted functional distances track empirical regime distances (Spearman 0.96). From one unlabeled image, the inferred behavior selects operating points as well as a non-deployable lookup that knows the true regime (macro-regime $F_1$ 0.6604 for both, versus 0.6407 under pristine calibration; oracle 0.6620). On this discrete benchmark, regime-supervised curve lookups are strong controls. Pre-specified continuous and compositional probing shows where functional inference matters: on unseen combinations, the functional decoder has a lower mean curve error than a template lookup, increasingly with distance from the training conditions, whereas the lookup is more accurate for interpolation. These results establish the feasibility of single-image inference of distribution-level detector behavior over the probed conditions. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/dobi

candidates.title: MedSkill-E$^{2}$: Evaluating and Evolving Skills for Medical Agents
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills to access domain knowledge and complete real-world tasks. We observe that even when a skill specifies the rules and procedures needed for a task, agents may fail to apply them effectively during autonomous execution, a phenomenon we call skill Enable But Underuse (EBU). This issue is particularly consequential in medical tasks, where overlooking a single critical constraint can yield a plausible but incorrect result. To evaluate and address EBU, we introduce MedSkill-E$^{2}$, a framework for evaluating and evolving skills for medical agents. We construct EBU-Bench, a challenging benchmark covering 12 medically relevant task groups and associated skills, to evaluate agents' ability to use available skills autonomously. We quantify the EBU gap as the difference in skill-use accuracy between autonomous use and explicitly guided reading and application of the same skill. On EBU-Bench, all evaluated model-harness combinations exhibit EBU, with a mean gap of 43.94 percentage points (pp). For the same model, skill-use accuracy under autonomous use differs by up to 38.96 pp across harnesses. Motivated by these observations, we propose EBU-Evolve, which uses execution feedback from autonomous and explicitly guided skill use to distill effective guidance into reusable skill instructions. Relative to their pre-evolution versions, the revised skills improve skill-use accuracy during autonomous execution by 33.33 to 55.17 pp and continue to yield improvements when transferred across multiple models and harnesses. Our results show that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies across harnesses with the model and skill held fixed, and model rankings can change. EBU can persist even after a skill is opened. EBU-Evolve improves autonomous skill-use accuracy on unseen tasks within the same skill, with gains transferring across models and harnesses.

candidates.title: Navigent: A Geometry-Grounded Agentic Framework for Vision Language Navigation
candidates.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. Project Page: https://marslab-navigent.github.io/navigent.github.io/ Code: https://github.com/MarsLab-Navigent/Navigent

candidates.title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.
candidates.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ESANN 2027. Code: https://github.com/kianaf/exposure-rl

candidates.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
candidates.abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.
candidates.comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery: Bridging the Translation Gap (AI4DD). Code and data: https://github.com/jackysiupuichung/forecast-or-know

candidates.title: Autonomous Vineyard Exploration using LiDAR Sensing: A Field Evaluation on Legged-Wheeled Quadruped Robot
candidates.abstract: Autonomous navigation in vineyards presents significant challenges due to uneven terrain, sparse vegetation, and the repetitive geometric nature of vineyard rows. This paper evaluates a LiDAR-based autonomous exploration system deployed on a Unitree Go2 Wheeled quadruped robot. Our approach utilizes an iterative RANSAC-based line detection pipeline to identify vineyard rows and a finite-state navigation strategy to govern row selection and traversal. Field evaluations conducted at Denbies Vineyard (UK) demonstrate the system's ability to perform sustained autonomous row following, completing a 370m up-and-down traversal without intervention. We analyze the failure modes encountered, specifically focusing on line detection instability in sparse vegetation and the trade-offs of spatial filtering. The results suggest that, while RANSAC provides a robust geometric primitive, additional temporal filtering and adaptive perception are required for reliable lane-to-lane transitions in commercial vineyard environments. A video of the experimental results is available at: youtu.be/1om1HFGF4ps

candidates.title: Patterns and correlations in time-reversal symmetry breaking
candidates.abstract: Time-reversal symmetry (TRS) breaking is the hallmark of non-equilibrium statistical physics. This notwithstanding, in translationally invariant systems, it is almost always treated only as a global quantity. We propose to use the local entropy production rate as a spatio-temporal field to describe extended homogeneous non-equilibrium systems. We find that this field generically displays spatial correlations, with a typical length that grows as we approach some non-equilibrium phase transitions. We also show that the correlation length associated with the local entropy production rate follows heretofore unknown scaling laws involving control parameters as well as the observation time used for trajectories. Our work paves the way to the use of the local entropy production as a powerful observable to identify the scale and source of TRS breaking in non-equilibrium systems.

candidates.title: Analemma $\infty$: A Temporal Benchmark for Geospatial Foundation Models
candidates.abstract: Satellite time series capture how land surfaces change over time. Pixel-wise temporal foundation models read a year of satellite observations per pixel, yet public benchmarks lack a temporal axis or subsample it to a few dates. We introduce Analemma, a temporal benchmark of six datasets that carry every 10 and 20 m Sentinel-2 band and a time series spanning a growing season, completed where their releases omit geometry, dates, or cloud masks. One frozen-encoder protocol evaluates all models across label ratios and three seeds, with two baselines without pretraining. The TESSERA model ranks first overall. A from-scratch model on monthly composites outranks every foundation model except OlmoEarth v1.3-Base, suggesting that temporal input explains most of the performance. Three evaluation choices left unstated by the source publications each shift TESSERA v1 by 7.6 to 18.6 mIoU, against top-two gaps of 0.6 to 2.8. Data, harness and leaderboard will be publicly released soon.
candidates.comment: 30 pages, 13 figures, 17 tables. Includes supplementary material

candidates.title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation
candidates.abstract: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.

candidates.title: AI, Automation, and Fiscal Pressure
candidates.abstract: We study how automation affects public finances in countries that (i) tax labor at a higher rate than capital and (ii) fund services such as health care and education from tax revenues rather than user fees. We embed task-level automation within a two-sector general equilibrium model, which we calibrate to match data from EU countries. Automation shifts income toward more lightly taxed capital. If public services follow consumer demand, the budget deficit worsens at unchanged tax rates, even if automation is as fast in the public-service sector as in the private sector. In our EU-27 benchmark scenario, where automation proceeds faster in the market sector, the deficit rises by nearly one percentage point of value added as the economy grows by twelve percent due to automation.

candidates.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
candidates.abstract: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.

candidates.title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
candidates.abstract: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

candidates.title: Evaluating Post-Quantum and Hybrid Signatures for Blockchains: Performance, Storage and Ledger Growth
candidates.abstract: Advances in quantum computing pose a long-term threat to blockchain systems that rely on classical digital signature schemes such as ECDSA. Migrating these systems to post-quantum cryptography introduces practical costs beyond cryptographic security, including larger transactions, higher computational costs and faster ledger growth. We present an empirical evaluation of 13 signature configurations in a common simulated blockchain framework: ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65/87, Falcon-512/1024, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s, and six hybrids combining ECDSA with each post-quantum scheme. We measure signing and verification costs, transaction-processing throughput, and signature and public-key sizes, and project the measured overheads onto five public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, BNB Smart Chain and TRON. Verification remains inexpensive for the evaluated lattice-based schemes, with Falcon-512 achieving a verification time comparable to ECDSA (30.1 versus 32.8 $μ$s). Storage overheads, however, are substantial. Under our modelling assumptions, had the recorded transaction histories used Falcon-512, the most compact post-quantum scheme evaluated, ledger sizes would have been 79--229% larger, depending on the blockchain. Hybrid configurations introduce relatively modest additional storage overhead compared with their standalone post-quantum counterparts, while ECDSA+Falcon-512 approximately doubles the verification cost of standalone Falcon-512. Existing transaction- and script-size limits also present obstacles to straightforward migration in Bitcoin and Solana. Overall, our findings suggest that storage overhead may pose a greater challenge than signature verification costs when migrating blockchain systems to post-quantum cryptography.

candidates.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
candidates.abstract: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.

candidates.title: LiveRelight: Sub-Second Global Illumination Editing for Gaussian Interiors
candidates.abstract: Relighting reconstructed 3D scenes remains challenging due to the complex nature of light transport: slow or approximate visual feedback restricts the editor's ability to fine-tune the results to satisfaction. We present a hybrid relighting approach that enables interactive, high-fidelity updates of direct and indirect indoor illumination without per-edit optimization. Our approach permits the editor to make a wide range of relighting edits at room-scale, with near-instant feedback. Our key insight is to precompute geometric light exchange rather than illumination responses, retaining an inexpensive transport solve that accommodates changes in emission and surface reflectance. We evaluate direct illumination on reconstructed 2D Gaussians using visibility-aware sampling of one-sided emitters, while propagating diffuse interreflection through sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy. A sparse projection fitted through Gaussian alpha compositing transfers the proxy solution to the reconstruction. Our formulation further supports fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion by recomputing light source injection. Across eight relighting conditions of our synthetic test suite, our sub-second edits improve relighting fidelity over prior path-traced editing by an average of 5\,dB PSNR, while reducing editing latency by up to three orders of magnitude. Qualitative results further demonstrate realistic, interactive relighting of real-world captures.

candidates.title: EgoMyo: Physical Hand State Estimation from Egocentric Video and Wrist Electromyography
candidates.abstract: Physical hand interaction depends on configuration, contact, and force, yet nearly identical appearances can conceal different contact states and exerted forces. We therefore formulate physical hand state estimation from egocentric video and wrist surface electromyography (sEMG), combining visual geometry with neuromuscular evidence to jointly recover these coupled components. To support this task, we introduce EgoMyo, a benchmark spanning 5.75M video frames, 50 participants, 34 contact configurations, and repeated donnings, synchronizing these inputs with 3D hand pose and with contact and normal force registered onto the hand surface from bare-hand pressure. Controlled analysis reveals that vision resolves spatial structure while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, that sEMG's gains concentrate in regions where vision is least reliable, and that contact localization limits force accuracy. Guided by these findings, we propose MyoBridge, which makes the hand region the unit of vision-sEMG fusion, lets each region gate its own share of sEMG, and distributes regional force magnitudes only over predicted contact vertices at inference. On held-out trials, MyoBridge reduces pose and force error by 39.8% and 18.5% over the strongest baseline and achieves the lowest pose error on unseen sessions and subjects.

candidates.title: AnyCam4D: Ray-Based 4D Gaussian Rendering for Arbitrary Camera Models
candidates.abstract: Real cameras are not pinholes, yet most dynamic Gaussian splatting assumes they are. Footage is therefore undistorted first, losing field of view or detail, especially with wide-angle and fisheye cameras. Static Gaussian splatting has largely solved this with ray-based rendering, which suits any camera. Native 4D Gaussians, which model motion in space-time, cannot use it directly: each Gaussian's orientation and size cannot be recovered reliably from its covariance. We present AnyCam4D, which trains native 4D Gaussians on original footage by ray-based rasterization, preserving field of view and resolution at about the per-step cost of standard projection. Our key contribution is a numerically stable way to obtain orientation and size: we condition a square root of the 4D covariance. Trained models render through other cameras, with rolling shutter, depth of field or chromatic aberration. With a synthetic 170-degree fisheye camera, training on original images improves peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 3.0-8.1 dB. On real footage, AnyCam4D has lower perceptual error than the standard projection adapted to each camera, at comparable PSNR and without camera-specific derivations. With the synthetic camera rotated 60-80 degrees away from the capture rig's view, it leads by 6.2 dB against ground truth.

candidates.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
candidates.abstract: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

candidates.title: Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for Self-Supervised Video Representation Learning
candidates.abstract: Self-supervised video representation learning has achieved remarkable progress by leveraging large-scale unlabeled video data. Recent methods commonly extend Masked Image Modeling (MIM) to Masked Video Modeling (MVM), where video representations are learned by capturing semantic information from temporal contexts during masked content recovery. Unlike static images, videos exhibit inherent temporal variation, as visual objects continuously change their positions, appearances, and motion states across frames. Therefore, MVM needs to preserve semantic consistency while capturing temporal changes of corresponding regions, which raises two central challenges: 1) how to establish reliable temporal correspondence across frames, and 2) how to formulate an appropriate representation learning objective for modeling both semantic consistency and temporal variation. To address these challenges, we propose Variation-aware Temporal Correspondence for video Representation learning (VT-CoRe) framework. For challenge 1), VT-CoRe introduces a sandwich sampling strategy to construct two-sided temporal references and a Patch Registration Module (PRM) to establish reliable patch-level correspondence. For challenge 2), VT-CoRe imposes latent-space semantic alignment on registered representations through a self-distillation architecture and further proposes temporal variation modeling to constrain representation trajectories over time. Experiments on 8 downstream tasks across 16 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of VT-CoRe across pixel-level, frame-level, video-level, and vision-based robotic learning scenarios. Complementary representation analysis shows that VT-CoRe learns a more structured latent space for variation-aware temporal correspondence learning.

candidates.title: Permutation tests for Poisson network regression: Double semi-partialling, studentized statistics and actor effects
candidates.abstract: The multiple regression quadratic assignment procedure (MRQAP) is a standard framework for inference on dyadic network data, and its properties are well established for the linear model. Network outcomes are often counts, modelled by Poisson regression with a log link. We prove that the invariance property of the Frisch--Waugh--Lovell theorem, the only part that double semi-partialling (DSP) requires, survives the nonlinear link. The DSP focal coefficient and its model-based, HC3 and dyadic cluster-robust standard errors coincide with those of the fit on the raw covariates. The choice between relabelling the raw focal array ($X$-permutation) and relabelling its DSP residual acts only on the reference distribution. The test holds its level when the relabelled designs reproduce the dependence that the statistic retains, and DSP reproduces the autocorrelation of the partialled focal covariate. When the raw focal array and its residual share their autocorrelation, the relabelling test holds the nominal level for all three statistics, at covariate correlations up to $0.9$ and in networks of $20$ to $100$ actors. A normal reference rejects a true null at rates up to $0.96$. With sender and receiver effects modelled, every statistic rejects a true null at $0.035$ to $0.070$ in all conditions, and power against a focal effect of $0.10$ rises from at most $32\%$ to at least $99.9\%$. When the actor effects cannot be modelled, adding the sender and receiver means of the nuisance covariates keeps DSP at its level. We give recommendations and illustrate the method on the EIES message-count network.

candidates.title: GeoCAM: Self-Supervised Sonar-Optical Representation Learning via Geographic Overlap Supervision
candidates.abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.
candidates.comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Advanced Visual and Signal-Based Systems (AVSS 2026)

candidates.title: Geometry, masking and selection in Differential Evolution and SOMA on quantum state manifolds
candidates.abstract: Differential Evolution (DE) and the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm (SOMA) generate new candidates through vector arithmetic: they subtract population members, scale the difference, and mask coordinates. Many practical search spaces are not vector spaces, however. Rotation angles are periodic, normalized states lie on spheres and projective spaces, and circuit parameters are coupled through the quantum states they produce. We present a systematic study of how such geometry affects the core operations of DE and SOMA. Keeping the operators and selection rules fixed, we replace only their geometric primitives and separate the effects of difference construction, masking, and selection in a large paired numerical study covering textbook manifolds and variational quantum problems. Geometry-consistent differences make full-crossover (CR = 1) DE significantly better on 16 of 31 non-Euclidean configurations, with no significant deterioration, and the advantage persists when the measured computational cost of each variant is taken into account. The effect is largest where ordinary subtraction misrepresents distances between candidates: success on periodic synchronization rises from 44% to 100%, and on a positive-definite matrix problem from 1% to 99%. On six- qubit variational eigensolvers, shortest-path angular differences reduce the mean final loss by 90% for about 3% extra runtime. The improvements come with two contrasting diversity patterns, more effective population contraction or preserved population diversity, so higher acceptance rates do not necessarily indicate better search. Crossover masks interact with geometry: they can favor cheaper retractions and can increase the distance moved in quantum-state space when circuit parameters are coupled. These results give practical rules for designing population-based optimizers on non-Euclidean and quantum search spaces.
candidates.comment: Submitted to Swarm and Evolutionary Computation for publication

candidates.title: PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence
candidates.abstract: When LLM agents verify each other's work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate feedback accumulating in memory. An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included. Code is available at https://github.com/Haochen-Luo/PROVE.

candidates.title: Beyond Gentrification: quantifying the economic, social and cultural dimensions of neighbourhood change through housing markets and digital traces
candidates.abstract: Neighbourhood change is a multidimensional process in which economic, demographic, social and cultural transformations do not necessarily coincide over space and time. However, data driven approaches typically collapse these into single indices or regression models, losing the nuances of individual components. This paper integrates housing market, demographic and social media data (SMD) to characterise different configurations of neighbourhood change in Leeds and Bradford, UK. Rates of change (2014-2019) were estimated over Lower Super Output Areas for house prices relative to the 250 nearest neighbouring areas, and for residential mobility, ethnic composition, unemployment and professional occupation. Approximately 1.6 million geo-tagged tweets, filtered for personal users using a large language model (LLM), were analysed using Structural Topic Models with socio-economic prevalence covariates, LLM based neighbourhood characterisation and text embeddings scored against gentrification and decline archetypes. These measures were used as inputs to a model-based cluster analysis, which identified six distinct neighbourhood types, and a spatially varying multinomial GAM was used to examine the effects of changes in the inputs on cluster membership. The results show repeated divergence between structural and discursive trajectories: rapid turnover that is invisible in local SMD discourse, heritage villages experiencing amenity and incomer pressure, a settled British-Pakistani community whose stability would be mis-characterised as stagnation or decline, and marginal areas accumulating strain with little on-line signal. This suggests that SMD derived measures can provide independent information on neighbourhood character rather than simply confirming structural indicators, although low SMD signals may reflect under-detection rather than an absence of change.

candidates.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
candidates.abstract: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

candidates.title: Graph-Informed Deep Factor Model for Statistical Arbitrage
candidates.abstract: Statistical arbitrage exploits temporary mispricings between similar assets in the cross-section of daily equity returns. We propose a nonlinear single-factor model, called a Graph-Informed Deep Factor (GIDF) model, whose per-stock loadings have cross-sectional dependence conditional on a latent network. The network captures cross-sectional return dependencies that remain after removing the dominant eigenmodes of the return correlation matrix, thereby providing a complementary representation of inter-asset relationships beyond the leading sources of systematic variation. It is reconstructed from data using a novel method that we call the Factor-Adjusted Dynamic EWMA (FADE). A signed-edge graph attention mechanism then combines the reconstructed network with exogenous firm characteristics and macroeconomic variables. This graph-informed specification is designed to produce residuals that more effectively separate idiosyncratic mean-reverting dynamics from cross-sectional co-movements, yielding economically useful signals for daily statistical arbitrage. In a comprehensive empirical study on daily U.S. equities from 2015 to 2024, GIDF outperforms classical factor models and state-of-the-art deep learning methods, achieving an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 1.78 under the canonical Avellaneda--Lee rule.

candidates.title: Beyond Logits: Coherent Hallucination Mitigation via Attention Contrastive Decoding
candidates.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) demonstrate impressive multimodal capabilities, yet suffer from hallucination - generating factually inaccurate content. Contrastive Decoding (CD) mitigates this by contrasting amateur and expert branches at the logit level. However, our investigation reveals that such logit-level interventions fundamentally compromise generation coherence, necessitating restrictive penalty constraints unrelated to hallucination suppression. We introduce Attention Contrastive Decoding (ACD), a training-free plug-in that complements logit-level CD by relocating part of the contrastive operations to the attention mechanism. Operating at an earlier stage of the forward pass, ACD performs smooth semantic-preserving interventions through an Adaptive Subtraction Strategy (ASS), which attenuates hallucination-associated attention patterns while amplifying critical visual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that combining ACD with existing CD methods (e.g., VCD+ACD) produces substantially more coherent outputs with further reduced hallucinations, eliminating restrictive penalties while enabling trustworthy multimodal generation.

candidates.title: Text-Conditioned Low-Rank Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models for Multimodal Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Time-series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable numerical forecasting priors. However, forecast-relevant information may be conveyed in text without being reflected in the observed series. Many multimodal forecasting methods integrate such context through model inputs or intermediate representations. We investigate a complementary mechanism: text-conditioned parameter adaptation. We propose Context-to-LoRA for Time Series (C2LoRA-TS), which encodes text and generates temporary Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) updates for selected weight matrices of a frozen TSFM. Both the numerical backbone and text encoder remain frozen, and the method exactly recovers the frozen TSFM output when context is absent. Evaluated on Time-MMD across nine domains and three TSFM architectures, C2LoRA-TS achieves lower aggregate forecasting error than the frozen-TSFM and Static LoRA baselines for every architecture and seed. Replacing the instance-specific text with a single globally fixed context degrades performance for every architecture. These results support text-conditioned parameter generation as a viable strategy for multimodal forecasting with frozen TSFMs.
candidates.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems: From Forecasting to World Modeling (FMTS 2026)

candidates.title: Compressing probabilistic almost-linear recurrent networks without refitting
candidates.abstract: Can a compressed recurrent network reuse its learned noise model? We applied finite-horizon balanced truncation to ten probabilistic almost-linear networks on delayed recall. Reducing 64 states to 32 without refitting met forecast tolerances for seven networks when balancing included rectifier inputs, compared with one using the readout alone. Including rectifier inputs improved agreement with the parent's mean-centred forecast distribution on all ten networks, with a median reduction in discrepancy of 65%. Compared with random directions, rectifier inputs reduced centred divergence on six networks and mean forecast error on all ten. Both full and reduced networks underestimated uncertainty on weak cues.
candidates.comment: 6 pages including references. Under review for ESANN 2027

candidates.title: Loop4D: Embodied World Modeling with 4D VAEs and Looped Diffusion Transformers
candidates.abstract: Predicting the outcomes of robotic manipulation requires modeling both visual appearance and evolving 3D geometry. This poses two challenges: video compression can obscure fine-grained robot motion, while jointly predicting RGB and geometry demands sufficient generative capacity. We introduce Loop4D, a framework that addresses these challenges through motion-preserving 4D representations and recurrent generative refinement. Our 4D VAE encodes RGB and pointmap sequences into compact spatiotemporal latents while preserving motion details and geometric structure. Our RGB VAE combines geometry-guided supervision with predictive reconstruction to reduce compression-induced motion artifacts. Our geometry VAE uses lightweight adapters to adapt pretrained RGB representations while preserving their priors. Building on these representations, our Dual-Stream Looped Diffusion Transformer maintains separate appearance and geometry streams with shared Transformer weights and cross-modal connections. By reusing Transformer blocks across loops, we increase effective depth without replicating backbone parameters, enabling models with fewer parameters to improve joint RGB-geometry prediction through additional computation. Experiments demonstrate high-quality 4D generation and validate Loop4D in simulated robotic manipulation tasks.

candidates.title: Time-consistency of cash-subadditive risk measures: The infimal cocycle property
candidates.abstract: We characterize the time-consistency of convex, cash-subadditive dynamic risk measures in terms of their minimal penalty. The dual variables are conditional sub-probability densities, which factorize across an intermediate date in many ways, according to how the discount is allocated to the two periods. We introduce an infimal cocycle property, in which the penalty is the infimum over all such factorizations, and show that it is equivalent to time-consistency, with the infimum attained. This holds on $L^\infty$ under continuity from below, and on $L^p$, $p<\infty$, without continuity assumptions. In the cash-additive case it reduces to the classical cocycle property. For risk measures induced by BSDEs, it represents the dynamic programming principle of a stochastic control problem whose value is the penalty.

candidates.title: Veronese Classification of Constant-Curvature Minimal Two-Spheres in Complex Hyperquadrics
candidates.abstract: We prove that every linearly full, irreducible conformal minimal immersion of constant Gaussian curvature and finite isotropy order from the two-sphere into a complex hyperquadric comes from a member of a Veronese sequence. The result holds at every finite isotropy order, without an unramifiedness or additional Frenet-norm polynomiality assumption. Both the associated projective harmonic sequence and the target harmonic sequence are totally unramified as consequences. If the replacement depth is \(\ell\) and the holomorphic seed spans \(\mathbb{CP}^m\), the curvature is \(K=2/((2\ell+1)m-2\ell^2)\) in the Grassmannian normalization. Real Gram data characterize the admissible embeddings and give an algebraic converse. The proof uses holomorphic Pfaffian norm identities, degree estimates that retain all ramification divisors, and a valuation argument that identifies the retained lines with seed Frenet lines.

candidates.title: SOLO: Towards Sample-Faithful and Detectable LLM Watermarking under Repeated Sampling via Content-Anchored Single-Owner Contexts
candidates.abstract: Providers watermark the outputs of large language models, while applications sample many responses per prompt for self-consistency, best-of-n selection, and uncertainty estimation. We show that deployed configurations of distortion-free watermarks, which deduplicate keyed contexts only within a response, couple the responses of a request: answer templates make all responses query the watermark with the same context before the answer, so collisions across responses, usually assumed rare, become the norm. Key pools reduce or avoid the coupling at the cost of multiple testing, and the exact remedy of a context history shared across the request leaves many positions unwatermarked. We propose SOLO, which keeps a request-scoped context history but anchors its keyed contexts on content selected by min-hash, so that siblings rarely compete for a context and random edits stay local. Its responses are jointly distributed as independent unwatermarked responses, each detectable with a single key. On five language models from three families and three benchmarks, SOLO preserves self-consistency and uncertainty estimation and, at a 1% false positive rate, detects more responses than four-token key pools on most tasks, also after randomly editing 10% of the tokens, and more than the context history on most clean tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/ZhongliangGuo/solo-watermark.

candidates.title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance
candidates.abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.
candidates.comment: To appear in Proceedings of EACL 2027 (Main conference paper)

candidates.title: A Local-Counting Approach for Distributed Induced Path Detection
candidates.abstract: A well-known application of the celebrated color-coding technique is fast detection of paths in a distributed setting with limited bandwidth, by propagating a signal along colorful paths [Even et al., DISC 2017]. However, since vertices of the same color are indistinguishable by this procedure, it cannot detect induced paths, as they appear the same as cycles. We make the following observation. If, for a given edge, we \emph{count} the number of such signals over all permutations of the random coloring that terminate at that edge, then we can separate an induced path from a cycle: an induced path contributes one to that count, while a cycle contributes two. Refining and generalizing this observation gives our \emph{local-counting approach}, which allows us to separate induced paths from any other subgraph. We establish the following end results, all improving upon the state of the art in their round complexities and refined detection variants. * An $O(1)$-round algorithm for induced $P_4$ detection. * $O(Δ)$-round algorithms for detection of induced $P_5$ and $P_6$. * An $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})$-round algorithm for detection of induced $P_5$ in induced-$C_4$ free graphs.

candidates.title: Hierarchical Semantic Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities
candidates.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.
candidates.comment: Accepted for Publication in IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (TMM), 2026

candidates.title: Lightweight Reasoning Transfer via Chain-of-Thought Vector Projection
candidates.abstract: Transferring reasoning capabilities from large language models to smaller ones often requires extensive teacher supervision or costly student adaptation. We study projected cross-model Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Vector transfer, a two-stage approach that keeps both models frozen. First, we learn a task-level CoT Vector in the teacher using dataset-provided solution traces and final-answer supervision. We then train a lightweight linear projector to map the fixed vector into a smaller student's residual space. Student-side training uses only final-answer cross-entropy on a small subset of task training examples; it requires neither teacher outputs nor intermediate solution traces. We select the student injection layer and intervention scale on a labeled support set and report results on the disjoint remainder of each evaluation split. On GSM8K and MATH, the projected vector improves base students by 10.37-21.98 accuracy points across the evaluated teacher-student settings. On four code-generation benchmarks, the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct student gains 3.23-4.67 pass@1 points, while the base Qwen2.5-7B student gains up to 9.65 points. These results show that a teacher-side reasoning vector can be reused across smaller students with different residual dimensions through projector-only adaptation.

candidates.title: Agentic-Level Adversarial Purification: Revisiting Diffusion Purifiers on Native-Resolution Agentic Inputs
candidates.abstract: Vision-language agents act on native-resolution renders of multi-element pages, where one perturbed photo or a few altered text strokes can redirect the decision. Any content provider can craft such a perturbation on the open model behind the agent, so a plug-in purifier is the natural first line of defense. Yet diffusion purifiers were designed and evaluated at the fixed resolution of the diffusion model on classifier or natural-image benchmarks, and defense evaluations for agents test JPEG, blur and noise but no diffusion purifier. We present the first study of adversarial purification at the agentic level, for an agent built on Qwen3-VL-8B: purifiers run at native resolution on multi-element inputs, face grey-box attackers who know the agent's model but not the defense, and are compared at matched clean cost. We show that treating agentic inputs as classifier inputs misleads both evaluation and design. Resizing the input to the resolution of the diffusion model, as existing purifiers do, raises the TextVQA clean cost of the Divide-and-Conquer purifier (DC) from 4.0 to 35.7 points. On web-shop pages, DC keeps 85.0% grey-box robust accuracy against web-hardened perturbations, where cheap input transformations at matched clean cost keep at most 40.0%, and this robustness comes from the global noise level: input-estimated masks and noise levels add none. These findings hold on a disjoint held-out set and on a second VLM and yield three requirements for defenses, we release the protocol.

candidates.title: Familiar Words, Unfamiliar Minds: Conventionalization without Calibration in the Vocabulary of Mind
candidates.abstract: Speakers describe new technologies by stretching old words, letting experience of the new referents sort out which inferences carry over. I argue that stretching the vocabulary of mind to language models pulls apart two processes that theories of metaphor and linguistic change tend to conflate: conventionalization, whereby a stretched word ceases to be marked as such, and calibration, whereby the inferences it invites are fitted to what its new referents bear out. As a gene variant can reach fixation without being an adaptation, a word can become conventional without being calibrated. A corpus study of "hallucinate" in 8,568 abstracts and 31,866 forum comments shows conventionalization running most of its course within three years. Calibration need not keep pace: these models are organized so unlike human minds that it is hard to tell when mental words apply and what they imply. Even warranted attributions can mislead: mechanistic analysis shows that a transformer trained to navigate Manhattan has and uses a faithful street map, yet loses track of its position on long, diverted journeys. Nor is the gap likely to close by itself. The usual routes to calibration (direct experience, designers' knowledge, experiment) presuppose a referent that is accessible, stable, and independent of the discourse about it. But language models are opaque, fast-changing, and looped into the discourse: they are trained on past uses of mental vocabulary and on the experimental literature about them, and join the discourse themselves. Calibration must therefore be organized, through a reciprocal, not merely deferential, division of linguistic labour. This yields a norm of targeted qualification (flag the specific inferences an attribution invites without support), a reply to the worry that meaning change eludes deliberate control, and three testable predictions about when qualifications calibrate expectations.

candidates.title: Semantic Tanner-Graph Decoding for LDPC Codes
candidates.abstract: Conventional low-density parity-check (LDPC) belief propagation (BP) decoding operates on a Tanner graph, with no factor describing the source structure. This paper proposes a semantic Tanner graph for LDPC-coded text transmission and develops semantic-factor-aided BP (SF-BP) decoding. The source text is tokenized into discrete tokens, which are then mapped to binary messages for channel coding. For each token, the proposed graph introduces a semantic factor connected to the corresponding information-bit variable nodes forming the token. A fine-tuned language model assigns this factor a posterior distribution over all possible token symbols in the alphabet at each token position. During SF-BP decoding, semantic-factor and LDPC parity-check messages are combined at their shared variable nodes for message passing. Simulation results show that SF-BP significantly improves the block error rate (BLER) and Sentence-BERT similarity (BERT: Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) compared with conventional BP. For example, SF-BP reduces BLER from approximately 1 to 6.51 x 10^-6 and increases Sentence-BERT similarity from 0.21 to 1 - 1.26 x 10^-6 for the (1248, 1040) LDPC code at 4 dB.
candidates.comment: 5 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in IEEE Communications Letters

candidates.title: Multi-view fnirs identifies neurophysiological subtypes in post-stroke aphasia
candidates.abstract: Post-stroke aphasia is clinically heterogeneous, and conventional classifications may not capture differences in brain functional organisation. We tested whether resting-state and task-based functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) could identify neurophysiological subgroups alongside clinical assessment.Seventy-nine patients underwent unsupervised clustering using three fNIRS feature views: resting-state activity and connectivity, language-task activation, and rest-to-task connectivity reconfiguration. Similarity network fusion and spectral clustering integrated the views. Clinical and behavioural measures were excluded from clustering.Three clusters (n = 32, 17 and 30) were identified. This solution had the largest eigengap and was the only candidate significant after permutation testing and Holm correction (adjusted P = 0.001). It was stable under subsampling (mean adjusted Rand index, 0.773), but agreement fell to 0.217 when the resting-state view was removed. Clusters differed in most regional intrinsic-activity measures and all resting-state connectivity summaries, with few differences in task activation or connectivity reconfiguration. Their profiles showed higher right anterior prefrontal activity, distributed fronto-sensorimotor and parietal alterations, and reduced interhemispheric connectivity, respectively.Cluster membership was not significantly associated with conventional aphasia subtype (Cramér's V = 0.287), and baseline clinical language scores and task performance did not differ between clusters.These findings identify three neurophysiological subgroups distinguished mainly by intrinsic activity and resting-state functional connectivity, not clearly aligned with conventional aphasia classifications or baseline clinical measures. Multi-view fNIRS analysis may complement clinical characterisation, requiring independent and longitudinal validation.

candidates.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
candidates.abstract: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.
candidates.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery (AI4DD). 5 pages main text, 28 pages total

candidates.title: Admoab-DETR: Resolution-Tiered Fusion for Infrared-Visible Object Detection with Missing Modalities
candidates.abstract: Infrared and visible images offer complementary cues for all-weather object detection, yet real-world sensor dropouts can leave one stream unavailable and degrade paired-input detectors. Meanwhile, existing modality-adaptive methods apply heavy cross-modal attention uniformly across scales, incurring prohibitive token overhead on high-resolution maps. We propose Admoab-DETR, a unified real-time detector supporting infrared-only, visible-only, and paired inputs with a single set of weights. Specifically, \emph{Resolution-Tiered Fusion} (RTF) allocates fusion capacity by spatial token density and feature granularity: a lightweight Spatial Modality Gate governs fine local fusion at the highest-resolution scale with zero-cost single-view pass-through, while channel-compressed deformable Admoab necks capture cross-modal correspondence at coarser semantic scales. Furthermore, \emph{Mode-Matched Feature Distillation} (MMFD) aligns multi-scale encoder features with an availability-synchronized full-fusion teacher, avoiding ill-posed cross-modal hallucination while cutting parameters by 18.1\% and paired latency by 39.6\% at zero inference overhead. We also construct Admoab, a strictly registered 20,000-pair infrared--visible benchmark across diverse scenes. Experiments show Admoab-DETR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy--efficiency trade-offs across missing-modality and paired benchmarks. Our code will be available at https://github.com/liwenchao0615/Admoab-DETR.

candidates.title: Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding for Temporally Grounded Audio-Visual Understanding
candidates.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) are designed to represent the temporal structure of audio and video, yet it remains unclear how effectively they use this temporal information to relate sounds to visual events. To examine this, we probe an AV-LLM on an audio-visual synchronization task by shifting the audio so that the queried sound overlaps a different visual event. We observe that the model still favors the originally aligned event over the newly aligned one, indicating limited sensitivity to changes in audio-visual temporal alignment. To address this, we propose Modality-Shift Contrastive Decoding (MSCD), a training-free decoding method that emphasizes audio-visual temporal alignment in model predictions. MSCD contrasts logits under preserved and disrupted temporal alignment to favor predictions supported by aligned audio and video. We disrupt this alignment by temporally shifting either the audio or the video, while keeping the other modality fixed. Extensive evaluations with two AV-LLMs across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MSCD for temporally grounded audio-visual understanding. In particular, MSCD improves accuracy over the base models on Daily-Omni by 2.2 and 2.8 percentage points for OmniVinci and video-SALMONN 2+, respectively, suggesting that emphasizing temporal alignment can also benefit broader audio-visual understanding.

candidates.title: CoordRoute: Coordinated Multi-Model Routing for Maximum Compute-Budget Utility
candidates.abstract: Model routing sends each request to one of several large language models (LLMs) of different sizes. In practice, requests share a fixed compute budget: a spending cap on rented model APIs or the capacity of a private GPU cluster. Most existing routers do not account for the total budget: each decides a request on its own, so per-request optima are not optimal overall. We advocate coordinated routing, which allocates the budget across requests to maximize its utility, their total satisfaction, along a predict-plan-rectify route: predict what each model would give and cost, plan the choice against later requests, and rectify it during generation. Each step faces a challenge: a request's gain from each model is uncertain before generation, later arrivals are unknown when a request must start, and observing answers during generation consumes the budget itself. CoordRoute addresses them with relative demand prediction, which compares candidate models through past requests that lead to the same routing choices; a lookahead solver, which charges each choice for what its compute could earn for later requests; and budget-aware runtime correction, which drops or upgrades in-flight requests at the same price, inspecting answers only when it pays off. On Azure Conversation and BurstGPT traces, CoordRoute improves total satisfaction by 18.72% over the strongest existing router.

candidates.title: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments
candidates.abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.

candidates.title: OceanFix: Reference-Guided Diffusion for Sparse-View Underwater 3D Reconstruction
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting have enabled efficient underwater reconstruction, but sparse observations, light attenuation, and backscatter still leave scene regions underconstrained and cause novel-view artifacts. We present OceanFix, a reference-guided framework for sparse-view underwater 3D reconstruction that combines diffusion-based view repair with Gaussian scene refinement. Our repair model follows a two-stage training strategy that separates underwater appearance adaptation from geometric refinement. The first stage learns underwater appearance from reference observations and estimated medium features. The second uses camera poses and reference depth to align reference features, with relative-depth supervision guiding structural repair without requiring target-view depth at inference. We further propose medium-aware distillation that transfers repaired views into the 3D scene according to geometric repair demand and channel-specific optical observability. Through iterative rendering, repair, and distillation, OceanFix refines underconstrained regions while retaining supervision from the observed views. Experiments on underwater datasets demonstrate that OceanFix improves rendering quality in sparse-view 3D reconstruction, reducing visible artifacts and recovering finer scene details.

candidates.title: When High Capacity Becomes Undeployable: Pore-Filling Constraints for Multi-Objective Optimization of Direct Air Capture Sorbents
candidates.abstract: Amine-impregnated sorbents with the highest nominal CO2 capacity are frequently the least deployable, as amine beyond the pore-volume limit blocks active sites. Yet multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) for direct air capture (DAC) treats formulation search as unconstrained. We encode the pore-filling boundary as an explicit outcome constraint, c(x) = tanh(1 - phi_hat) - tau, and use it as a diagnostic instrument on a hand-curated, DOI-traceable benchmark of 618 solid-amine formulations from 43 publications. Unconstrained MOBO attains higher nominal capacity (3.639 +/- 0.815 vs. 2.964 +/- 0.728 mmol/g, p = 1.0e-11), but across 100 seeds 63.2% of its Pareto-optimal candidates violate the pore-filling boundary versus 39.3% under the constraint: it is rewarded for proposing candidates outside the pore-confined design regime. The constraint steers the front to lower loadings (55.8 vs. 65.2 wt%) and larger pores. The boundary is corroborated once apparatus effects are harmonized hierarchically: 77.8% of kinetic variance is between-laboratory, and pore filling carries a significant kinetic penalty (p = 0.002). Standard hypervolume over-credits feasibility-agnostic methods by 13.9-16.1% (vs. 11.1% constrained), and three surrogate-based analyses---the constrained front, a regeneration-energy third objective, and harmonized kinetics---consistently point to a conservative deployable window at pore filling phi_hat ~ 0.4-0.5 (45-55 wt% loading). The benchmark and associated analysis outputs accompany this submission.

candidates.title: HSTTA: Hierarchical Selective Test-Time Adaptation for Label-Free Cross-Subject EEG-to-Image Retrieval
candidates.abstract: Cross-subject EEG-to-image retrieval suffers from substantial performance degradation on new subjects due to subject shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this shift by adapting pretrained models with unlabeled target-subject EEG. However, most existing TTA methods struggle to match supervision granularity to each query's prediction confidence, leaving many queries without reliable pseudo-labels. To address this, we propose a novel framework named Hierarchical Selective Test-Time Adaptation (HSTTA). HSTTA builds a hierarchy over gallery image embeddings, uses hierarchical selective prediction to assign each EEG query a supervision granularity matching its current prediction confidence, and constructs adaptation objectives accordingly. We further propose Cross-Session Consistency Calibration (CSCC), an unsupervised method that calibrates the global confidence threshold to target a predefined accuracy level for hierarchical predictions. Moreover, we introduce Reciprocal Hierarchical Backoff (RHB), which moves queries lacking reverse-matching support to coarser nodes to mitigate error reinforcement. Experiments on two public benchmarks and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of HSTTA and its key components. On THINGS-EEG2, HSTTA outperforms the strongest EEG-specific TTA baseline by 17.9 (13.4) and 8.9 (3.7) percentage points in Top-1/Top-5 accuracy, respectively, under cosine (CSLS) ranking. Further analyses show that HSTTA yields more accurate pseudo-labels during adaptation, supporting more reliable model updates.

candidates.title: Lost in the Grid: Where Multimodal LLMs Fail Between Seeing and Planning
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at static visual understanding and are increasingly applied to spatial planning, where a model interprets a visual layout and outputs an action sequence to reach a goal. Grid games are a common testbed for this ability because their rules are explicit and a solver can verify every move. Yet existing benchmarks mostly report end-to-end success rates, which hide whether a failure stems from visual perception, rule application, or multi-step planning. We introduce GridProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that 1) locates the failing stage between visual perception and planning and 2) verifies the diagnosis by targeted fine-tuning. On Sokoban, GridProbe pairs end-to-end solving with four probes (recognition, localization, single-step prediction, and state tracking) and gives every board both as an image and as an equivalent text grid. Evaluating seven MLLMs on Sokoban and a maze game reveals distinct bottlenecks behind similar success rates: proprietary models are limited by multi-step planning, whereas open-source models are limited by rule application or by visual grid indexing, i.e., counting rows and columns. Planning failures also hide perception failures: when planning is easier, the visual cost of the same model grows from 7.6 to 37.7 points. The diagnosis identifies what to train: fine-tuning only the vision module of the perception-limited model on board reading raises its interactive Sokoban success 3.5-fold (5.8% to 20.4%) and transfers zero-shot to the unseen maze game (single-turn success 13.8% to 67.1%), whereas the same data does not help a rule-limited model and training on solver solutions brings no gain. We will release the benchmark and code at https://github.com/suat-llm/GridProbe.

candidates.title: Counting complex elliptic curves with self-quotients via class numbers
candidates.abstract: Let \(n>1\) be an integer. We consider complex elliptic curves \(E\) admitting a finite subgroup \(C\subset E(\mathbb C)\) of order \(n\) such that \(E/C\) is isomorphic to \(E\). % with the additional requirement that the invariant factors of (C) are unequal. We establish class-number counting formulas for the cyclic, noncyclic, and general cases. More precisely, we associate to every negative quadratic-order discriminant \(D\) the norm form \[ Q_D(x,y)=x^2+\varepsilon_Dxy+q_Dy^2, \] where \[ \varepsilon_D\in\{0,1\},\qquad q_D=\frac{\varepsilon_D^2-D}{4}. \] The invariant factors of the kernel of the corresponding endomorphism are determined by \(\gcd(x,y)\). This leads to finite sets of admissible discriminants describing the cyclic, noncyclic, and general cases with unequal invariant factors. Our main result expresses the numbers of isomorphism classes in the three cases as sums of the proper ideal class numbers \(h(D)\) over explicitly defined finite sets of admissible discriminants. This provides an arithmetic class-number counting formulation of the CM classification developed in earlier work by \cite{CanepaGaba2014,CanepaGaba2019,CanepaGabaOlteanu2022} and its subsequent algorithmic extensions. We also characterize the equal-invariant-factor case: it occurs precisely when $n=m^2$, and in that case every complex elliptic curve satisfies the required condition, with the unique subgroup being $E[m]$. We derive an explicit bound for the admissible discriminants, implement the counting procedure in Magma, and give numerical examples. The proof relies on the Smith normal form of the multiplication matrix associated with a quadratic integer. The results provide an arithmetic class-number counting formulation of the CM classification developed in earlier work.

candidates.title: Ground Your Steps: Optimizing Sampling Schedules in Flow Matching Robot Policies
candidates.abstract: Flow matching robot policies generate action chunks by integrating a learned velocity field at inference. However, under a fixed budget of neural function evaluations (NFEs), the integration result depends on the sampling schedule. This motivates optimizing the schedule to bring the generated action distribution closer to the demonstrations and improve task success. We propose Ground Your Steps (GYS), a training-free method that optimizes the sampling schedule by matching the generated and demonstrated chunk distributions at each observation. GYS applies truncated fractional differencing along each arm joint's action sequence and compares two types of pairwise differences between action chunks at each observation: differences of a generated chunk against a demonstration, and differences of two independent generated chunks against each other.
